item.content:encoded:
- MLB. La última apertura de Justin Verlander marca el final de una carrera brillante
- MLB. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. consigue uno de los sencillos productores más extraños del béisbol
Los New York Mets no solo se quedaron fuera de los playoffs en 2026. Se desplomaron. Con un récord de 74-88, un último lugar en la División Este de la Liga Nacional y una de las nóminas más altas de las Grandes Ligas, la temporada terminó siendo un completo fracaso. Las lesiones, una construcción deficiente del roster y el bajo rendimiento general fueron factores importantes, por lo que no toda la responsabilidad puede recaer sobre dos jugadores.
Sin embargo, la rendición de cuentas debe comenzar con quienes estaban llamados a liderar al equipo. Francisco Lindor debía ser el corazón de la franquicia, mientras que Jorge Polanco llegó como un bateador veterano confiable. En cambio, ambos terminaron simbolizando una campaña en la que el talento más caro y probado estuvo muy lejos de responder a las expectativas de Nueva York.
Francisco Lindor nunca jugó como la estrella franquicia que esperaban los Mets
Lindor merece cierto contexto. Se sometió a una cirugía en el codo durante el invierno, sufrió una fractura del hueso ganchoso de la mano durante los entrenamientos y posteriormente estuvo cerca de dos meses fuera por una distensión en la pantorrilla. Con tantas interrupciones, encontrar ritmo fue prácticamente imposible.
Aun así, los Mets necesitaban una superestrella, no solo un jugador disponible en la alineación, y pocas veces la tuvieron. Lindor bateó para .225, con un porcentaje de embasado (.309), slugging (.423) y un OPS de .732, el más bajo de toda su carrera. Conectó 21 cuadrangulares, pero apenas produjo 49 carreras impulsadas en 105 juegos.
Su retroceso no se limitó al bate. Cometió 11 errores, la mayor cifra de su carrera, y terminó por debajo del promedio en la métrica Outs Above Average de Statcast. Un análisis sobre el rendimiento de los Mets de un año a otro mostró que su aporte cayó de 6.1 WAR en 2025 a una proyección de apenas 1.9 WAR en 2026, la mayor disminución entre las principales figuras que regresaron al equipo.
Nada de esto convierte a Lindor en un mal jugador, y las lesiones fueron un factor real. Pero cuando una franquicia está construida alrededor de un campocorto superestrella, perder más de cuatro victorias de valor esperado puede hundir una temporada. Los Mets confiaban en tener una ventaja clara en el shortstop y terminaron sin estabilidad ni excelencia en ambos lados del terreno.
Jorge Polanco fue el mayor problema de la alineación
Si Lindor representó la mayor decepción por las expectativas que existían sobre él, Jorge Polanco fue quien más perjudicó al equipo por sus resultados. Los Mets le otorgaron un contrato de dos años y 40 millones de dólares después de que conectara 26 cuadrangulares y registrara un OPS de .821 con Seattle en 2025, esperando que aportara profundidad y poder al lineup.
Lo que recibieron fue una de las peores temporadas ofensivas de todo el béisbol: promedio de .148, porcentaje de embasado de .201, slugging de .230, apenas dos jonrones y seis carreras impulsadas en 145 apariciones al plato. Además, fue utilizado casi exclusivamente como bateador designado, por lo que tampoco pudo compensar su bajo rendimiento con el guante. Tanto FanGraphs como Baseball Reference lo evaluaron con -1.4 WAR pese a disputar un número limitado de juegos.
Las lesiones en la muñeca, el tendón de Aquiles y el tobillo lo acompañaron durante toda la campaña, hasta que una cirugía en el tobillo puso fin a su temporada en agosto. Eso explica parte del desplome, pero no su impacto. Un bateador designado existe para producir ofensivamente, y Polanco ocupó un lugar en la alineación sin aportar poder, promedio ni capacidad para embasarse.
La oficina principal también merece críticas por construir un roster frágil, y las lesiones nunca dejaron de aparecer. Aun así, Lindor y Polanco sobresalen porque su producción estuvo muy por debajo del rol que debían desempeñar. La falta de liderazgo de Lindor le quitó a los Mets la base de su proyecto, mientras que el bate de Polanco convirtió una de las principales inversiones del invierno en un peso muerto. Ellos no fueron los únicos responsables de las 88 derrotas, pero sí representan mejor que nadie por qué un equipo diseñado para competir terminó hundido en el último lugar.

Welcome back to this season’s final edition of Monday Stat Party, a weekly series showcasing some of the most curious and nostalgia-inducing statistical developments from the past week of Mets baseball. What unites each entry is the sense of intrigue which they aim to spark, and the unbridled love of the game’s anomalies from which they arise. Without further ado, let the stat party begin.
TUESDAY
With his 25th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing broke Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
Kodai Senga became one of just 11 Japanese-born players to reach eight career saves, joining: Kazuhiro Sasaki (129), Koji Uehara (95), Takashi Saito (84), Akinori Otsuka (39), Shigetoshi Hasegawa (33), Shingo Takatsu (27), Hideki Irabu (16), Hisanori Takahashi (10), Masanori Murakami (9), and Yoshihisa Hirano (8).
Francisco Alvarez and Carson Benge each hit two doubles, marking the first time multiple Mets hit multiple doubles in a game since Ronny Mauricio and Jeff McNeil did it on July 27, 2025, in San Francisco.
WEDNESDAY
Marcus Semien hit his 15th home run of the year, giving the Mets six or more players with 15+ homers for the fifth time in franchise history after 2000 (7), 2017 (8), 2019 (6), and 2025 (6). The only teams with more 15-homer players this season were the Cubs, Reds, and Dodgers (all tied at 7). Of the Mets’ players with 15+ homers last season and this season, only two (Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto) overlap.
Juan Soto reached base four times for the 103rd time in his career, moving past Ted Williams for the third-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Mickey Mantle (121) and Jimmie Foxx (112).
Soto became the fifth Met to get intentionally walked three times in a game, after Claudell Washington (August 26, 1980), Vince Coleman (August 10, 1992), Todd Hundley (June 28, 1997), and David Wright (May 19, 2007, and July 18, 2009).
Brett Baty’s 455-foot home run tied the longest blast of his big league career, a homer off Brad Lord on August 20, 2025, in Washington.
Francisco Alvarez’s seventh-inning single registered an exit velocity of 113.7 mph. It was Alvarez’s 15th career batted ball with an exit velocity of 112+ mph, the second-most by a Met player in the Statcast era (since 2015) behind Pete Alonso, who had a whopping 130.
Alvarez, Lindor, and Baty each recorded a batted ball with an exit velocity over 110 mph, marking the first time the Mets recorded three batted balls with an exit velocity of 110+ mph in the same game since September 10, 2025, in Philadelphia.
Nolan McLean completed his rookie year with a total of 179.2 innings pitched, the most by a Mets rookie since Jae Weong Seo (188.1 in 2003), and 194 strikeouts, the third-most by a Mets rookie behind Dwight Gooden (276 in 1984) and Kodai Senga (202 in 2023).
McLean recorded his 250th strikeout in his 39th career game, tying Jacob deGrom for the fifth-fewest games by a Met to reach that milestone behind Dwight Gooden (29 games), Matt Harvey (34 games), Noah Syndergaard (36 games), and Kodai Senga (38 games).
McLean recorded his 26th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since deGrom (29) and Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
McLean became the first rookie with 20 quality starts since the Royals’ Yordano Ventura (22 in 2014). McLean’s 20 quality starts this season were tied with Sonny Gray and Cam Schlittler for fifth-most in the majors behind Cristopher Sánchez (22), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (22), Sandy Alcantara (21), and Michael Wacha (21). McLean also recorded his 21st start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
THURSDAY
Zac Thornton’s 63 strikeouts through 15 career games ranks fourth among Mets left-handers, behind Steven Matz (87), Bill Pulsipher (74), and David Peterson (69).
Juan Soto became the second Mets player to get intentionally walked four times in a two-game span, after Travis d’Arnaud did it while batting in the No. 8 spot ahead of Jon Niese and Bartolo Colón on June 1-2, 2014, in Philadelphia.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 63rd time this season. That ties 2013 for the most such games the Mets have had in a season in the Wild-Card Era (since 1995).
Over the franchise’s first five trips to Arlington, the Mets are still yet to lose a series on the road against the Rangers. They won two of three in 2003, won two of three in 2011, split a two-game set in 2017, won two out of three in 2024, and won two out of three again in 2026.
FRIDAY
Carson Benge became the first Mets rookie with 20+ homers and 20+ stolen bases in a season.
Benge became just the eighth player in MLB history to join the 20/20 club in their debut season, joining: Jackson Chourio (2024), Anthony Volpe (2023), Bobby Witt Jr. (2022), Julio Rodríguez (2022), Marty Cordova (1995), Ellis Burks (1987), and Mitchell Page (1977). (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Benge recorded his 43rd multi-hit game of the season, breaking Pete Alonso’s 2019 record for the most multi-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
With a pinch-hit single in the eighth inning, Brett Baty extended his career-high 18-game on-base streak. It was snapped with an 0-for-4 performance on Saturday.
Bo Bichette hit his fourth home run at Nationals Park this season, tied for the most by a Mets player in any season on the road against the Nats/Expos. His six extra-base hits trail only David Wright (7) in 2012.
Francisco Lindor didn’t notch his 300th home run on Friday night, but he did record three batted balls in a game at 107+ mph for the first time in the Statcast era (since 2015). Unfortunately for him, only one of the three resulted in a base hit.
The Mets allowed five wild pitches in a game and four wild pitches in an inning for the first time in franchise history.
SATURDAY
Jonah Tong set career highs with nine strikeouts and 19 whiffs in a game.
Mets pitchers recorded 14 or more strikeouts in a game for the 12th time this season, the fourth-most such games in a season in franchise history behind 2021 (19), 2019 (17), and 2022 (17).
With a start at shortstop, Brett Baty became the first Mets player to play six different positions in a season since Jeff McNeil in 2023.
Nate Lavender has recorded 19 scoreless appearances in his first 21 career outings, tied with Jaime Cerda, Erik Goeddel, and Daniel Zamora for the second-most by a Met behind Joe Smith (20).
In the Mets’ penultimate game of the season, their No. 8 and No. 9 hitters hit back-to-back homers (A.J. Ewing and Ronny Mauricio). The 2026 Mets had done that once before — in their first game of the season, when Carson Benge and Francisco Alvarez went deep at Citi Field against the Pirates.
The Mets clinched their sixth consecutive victory in the season series with Washington. Their record against the Nationals is 57-33 over that span.
SUNDAY
Francisco Lindor became the fifth player to hit their 300th career home run while having played at least 50% of their games at shortstop, joining Ernie Banks, Cal Ripken Jr., Alex Rodriguez, and Miguel Tejada. (source: Sarah Langs on X) He is also the 11th switch-hitter to reach the 300-homer mark. (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Lindor became one of 27 players with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, and the third active player to have reached the milestone along with Andrew McCutchen and Mike Trout. He is the fifth member of that club to have played for the Mets; the others were Willie Mays, Darryl Strawberry, Gary Sheffield, and Carlos Beltrán.
Lindor became the seventh player to hit their 300th home run as a Met, joining Dave Kingman, George Foster, Gary Carter, Mike Piazza, Mo Vaughn, and Curtis Granderson.
Lindor’s 300th homer registered a 110.8-mph exit velocity, marking the third-hardest-hit homer as a right-handed batter in his career. His only harder-hit homer from the right side as a Met came on another afternoon in Washington, when he took MacKenzie Gore deep on August 21, 2025.
Ronny Maurcio became the first Met to hit three consecutive homers out of the No. 9 spot, with two on Saturday and one on Sunday. (source: SNY broadcast)
Carson Benge recorded his 14th three-hit game of the season, extending his record for the most three-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
Juan Soto holds a 1.101 OPS against the Nationals in 39 games played facing his former team. That’s the third-highest OPS for any player with at least 150 plate appearances against the Nationals/Expos, trailing only Jim Edmonds (1.198) and Todd Helton (1.114).
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Let’s talk about the rookies.
In Carson Benge, Nolan McLean, A.J. Ewing, and Zac Thornton, the Mets have four rookies with at least 1.5 bWAR*. That’s tied for the most rookies with 1.5+ bWAR* in a season in franchise history, matching the mark from 1983 (Darryl Strawberry, Carlos Diaz, Walt Terrell, and Doug Sisk).
In Benge, McLean, and Ewing, the Mets have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*. Prior to this year, they had never had as many as two such rookies in a single season. In fact, the 2026 Mets are just the third team in the modern era (since 1900) to have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*, joining:
2006 Marlins (4: Hanley Ramírez, Dan Uggla, Josh Johnson, and Aníbal Sánchez)
1989 Orioles (3: Randy Milligan, Bob Milacki, Gregg Olson)
*bWAR separated for position players and pitchers, not cumulative
Thank you for following along all year! Here’s to many more stat parties in 2027…

item.content:encoded:
Juan Soto did not need a long answer when asked why the New York Mets can contend in 2027. After a 74-88 season that kept them out of the MLB playoffs, Soto gave a two-word answer: Carson Benge.
That is quite an endorsement for a rookie who just finished his first major league season.
The Mets entered 2026 with much bigger expectations, but injuries and an inconsistent roster eventually caught up with them. They finished last in the NL East and missed the postseason for the second straight year.
Benge, however, gave the club something it desperately needed: a reason to look forward.
The rookie finished with a .282 batting average, 20 home runs, 65 RBI, 168 hits and 22 stolen bases, according to the supplied 2026 statistics. SNY also reported that Benge became the first Mets rookie to reach 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases.
Juan Soto sees Carson Benge as part of the Mets’ future
Soto’s answer carries even more weight because he knows what the Mets need to fix.
The superstar played 111 games and hit .275 with 27 home runs, 68 RBI, a .393 on-base percentage and a .515 slugging percentage. But two calf injuries cost him significant time during the season, including a lengthy absence in July and August.
Soto has also said the Mets need to be active this offseason and add to their young core. He specifically pointed to Benge and other young players as reasons to believe the organization is moving in the right direction.
That puts plenty of attention on Benge heading into 2027. Not bad for a rookie who just finished his first trip around the league. Queens may have had a rough 2026, but at least Benge gave Mets fans something worth circling on the calendar.
The Mets still have work to do. Soto and Francisco Lindor provide veteran star power, but the pitching staff and overall roster need improvement after a 74-88 finish.
For now, though, Soto has made his choice clear when it comes to the biggest reason for optimism.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

28 Sep 2026, 10:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Ed Szczepanski)
Rookie Lucas Spence ripped a two-run triple to highlight a four-run third inning, helping the Houston Astros celebrate the American League West title with a 9-0 victory over the Athletics on Sunday in West Sacramento, Calif.
Christian Walker homered to lead off the sixth inning and joined Yainer Diaz, Cam Smith and Jeremy Pena in collecting two hits and an RBI for the Astros (81-81), who won the division for the eighth time in the last 10 seasons.
Third-seeded Houston will host the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Game 1 of the best-of-three wild-card series. The Astros went 5-2 against the White Sox this season.
Houston actually captured the AL West title prior to the conclusion of its victory, as the Texas Rangers dropped a 6-4 decision to the Minnesota Twins on Sunday.
Yordan Alvarez went 1-for-4 with an RBI single to boost his batting average to .316, giving him his first batting title.
Lawrence Butler had two of the five hits for the Athletics (64-98), who lost for the ninth time in 12 games.
Phillies 7, Tampa Bay 3
Zack Wheeler pitched six strong innings and Kyle Schwarber drove in two runs as the Phillies clinched their fifth straight postseason berth by beating the Rays.
Bryce Harper and Edmundo Sosa homered for Philadelphia, which had lost its previous four games by the combined score of 23-3. The Phillies finally showed signs of life in Game 162, and now they'll head to Atlanta to face the Braves in the National League wild-card round that begins on Tuesday,
Johnny DeLuca homered twice for Tampa Bay. The Rays earned a bye into the American League Division Series and face the winner of the wild-card series between the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox.
Cubs 6, Red Sox 2
Alex Bregman went 4-for-4 with two home runs and four RBIs against his former team to help Chicago wrap up the regular season by defeating Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The game was scheduled to be played in Boston, but was moved to Tropicana Field because of the nor'easter that hit much of New England throughout the weekend.
Both of Bregman's home runs came against Boston starter Tanner Houck, who made his first appearance on the mound since May 2025. Houck (0-1), who had Tommy John surgery last year, allowed three runs on four hits in three innings. The Red Sox were held to five hits and were 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position.
Twins 6, Rangers 4
Josh Bell hit a two-run home run and drove in three to lead host Minnesota to a season-ending win over Texas.
The loss eliminated the Rangers from the American League West title race and the playoffs. Rangers starter Mackenzie Gore allowed one hit and one run in 2 1/3 innings.
Twins starter Dean Kremer (5-5) gave up three hits and one run in seven innings. Kremer yielded a home run to Danny Jansen, but did not allow another Texas runner past first base.
Dodgers 5, Giants 1 (10 innings)
Andy Pages capped a four-run 10th inning with a three-run home run, and visiting Los Angeles beat San Francisco to earn its 100th win of the season.
The Dodgers took the lead in the 10th when Alex Call's two-out double off the left field fence drove in automatic runner Miguel Rojas. The Giants then elected to walk Max Muncy, before Pages foiled that strategy by driving a pitch by Duncan Davitt (0-1) into the left field bleachers for his 23rd home run of the season.
Alex Vesia (3-1), whose perfect ninth sent the game into the 10th, was credited with the win, which allows the Dodgers to take a three-game winning streak into their National League Division Series opener next Saturday against the winner of the wild-card series between the host Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
Marlins 5, Braves 3
Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine slugged solo home runs, giving host Miami a win over Atlanta to end its season on a high note.
Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara tossed a scoreless ninth inning for his third career save. It was a fitting end of the year for Alcantara, who threw both the first and last pitch of the season for Miami. sStarter Janson Junk left with a no-decision. He allowed three hits and one run in 4 2/3 innings. Michael Petersen (4-4) earned the win with 1 1/3 hitless innings of relief.
Braves starter JR Ritchie (1-5) took the loss. He allowed seven hits and four runs in 5 2/3 innings. Mauricio Dubon hit his 12th homer to open the scoring and added an RBI single for Atlanta, which begins its home wild-card series against divisional rival Philadelphia on Tuesday.
Nationals 6, Mets 4
Andres Chaparro had three hits, including two solo home runs, and host Washington beat New York to end its season with a series win.
Will Dion (3-2) pitched two scoreless innings for the victory and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his fifth save for Washington, which improved by 11 wins over 2025.
Francisco Lindor hit his 300th career homer and Ronny Mauricio smacked his third home run in two games for the Mets, who finished last in the National League East. Carson Benge ended his rookie season with three hits and an RBI.
Blue Jays 5, Reds 1
In potentially his final career start, Max Scherzer struck out seven over seven-plus innings and host Toronto topped Cincinnati.
The 42-year-old Scherzer (4-9) allowed one run and six hits to earn his 225th career win and boost his strikeout total to 3,557. The Blue Jays' 37-year-old designated hitter George Springer, who might have also played his last game, like Scherzer received a standing ovation when he was replaced.
Brandon Valenzuela hit a two-run home run for Toronto and Charles McAdoo added a solo shot in the rubber match of the three-game series. Brandon Williamson (5-5) allowed four runs and four hits in three innings for the Reds.
White Sox 4, Rockies 2
Randal Grichuk and Brenton Doyle smacked two-run home runs and Anthony Kay pitched five strong innings to boost host Chicago past Colorado.
The White Sox are set to visit the American League West champion Houston Astros on Tuesday in the opener of an AL wild-card series. Chicago clinched its first playoff berth on Thursday since 2021 but was eliminated from contention for an AL Central title with Saturday's loss to Colorado and a Cleveland victory at Kansas City.
Cole Carrigg homered for Colorado, which finished with more than 100 losses for the fourth successive season.
Royals 3, Guardians 2
Vinnie Pasquantino's second solo homer of the day broke an eighth-inning tie and sent host Kansas City to a win over Cleveland.
Jac Caglianone and Kyle Isbel each had two hits for the Royals, who ended a disappointing 2026 campaign by avoiding a sweep and winning for just the seventh time in the final 25 games.
Daniel Schneemann and Jo Adell each homered and had two hits apiece for the Guardians, who rested key regulars Steven Kwan, Jose Ramirez and Brayan Rocchio one day after securing their third consecutive American League Central title. Cleveland plays either the Chicago White Sox or Houston Astros in the American League Division Series.
Pirates 4, Tigers 2
Jared Jones pitched four innings of one-hit ball and Konnor Griffin led off the game with a solo home run and drove in two runs to lead Pittsburgh past host Detroit.
Griffin's homer was the sixth of his rookie season and helped the Pirates secure their first winning record since 2018 and only their second since last making the postseason in 2015. Jones was not eligible for the win after exiting the game before the fifth. Jones finished 5-6 with a 3.72 ERA in 21 starts after returning from elbow surgery in late May.
Rookie River Ryan (0-1) made his second start for the Tigers and sixth of his career. The right-hander allowed two runs on three hits over 1 1/3 innings. Detroit finished with a losing record after advancing to the American League Division Series each of the past two seasons.
Padres 9, Diamondbacks 4
Gavin Sheets homered and Freddy Fermin knocked in three runs as host San Diego tuned up for their National League wild-card series by stopping visiting Arizona.
San Diego, which opens its best-of-three series Tuesday night against the visiting Chicago Cubs, snapped a 4-4 tie with three runs in the bottom of the seventh. Fermin capped it with a two-run single.
Michael Soroka pitched 4 2/3 innings for Arizona, which was eliminated from postseason contention when Philadelphia beat Tampa Bay around the same time San Diego's Jake Cronenworth drew a bases-loaded walk to push home the go-ahead run in the seventh.
Brewers 6, Cardinals 4
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his case for the National League Cy Young Award, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as host Milwaukee beat St. Louis to close with five consecutive wins and its franchise record for victories in a season (103).
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings and lowered his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. The right-hander struck out five, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Cardinals starter Andre Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings. He allowed six singles in the first inning for a 3-0 Brewers lead as well as Gary Sanchez's home run in the third.
Mariners 7, Angels 4
Logan Gilbert pitched four-plus hitless innings and struck out eight as host Seattle dealt Los Angeles its 100th loss of the season. It was also the last game for Dan Wilson as the Mariners' manager. The team announced after the game that Wilson will not return in that role in 2027 after a disappointing season and third-place finish in the American League West.
Jose Siri homered for the Angels, losers of 100 games for the first time. They had been the lone active MLB team to never suffer that many defeats.
Gilbert didn't allow a baserunner until walking Moises Ballesteros leading off the fifth. He struck out the side in the first inning to reach 200 strikeouts for the season, becoming the fourth pitcher in franchise history to do so in multiple seasons.

WASHINGTON -- Francisco Lindor had been waiting to reach the 300-home run milestone for a while now. The Mets’ star shortstop was riding a 13-game homerless streak into Game 162 against the Nationals. He had last hit a long ball on Sept. 12, when he actually launched two homers out of Yankee Stadium.
But Lindor didn’t have to wait too much longer once the season’s last game finally got underway after a one-hour rain delay at Nationals Park on Sunday.
Lindor launched career home run No. 300 in the top of the second inning during the Mets' 6-4 loss to the Nationals. His 21st of the season came off Nationals left-hander DJ Herz, traveling a Statcast-projected 409 feet to left field at 110.8 mph off the bat.
Per the Elias Sports Bureau, Lindor is the fifth player to have played at least 50 percent of his games at shortstop at the time of his 300th home run, joining Ernie Banks, Cal Ripken Jr., Alex Rodriguez and Miguel Tejada.
Lindor also became the 11th switch-hitter with at least 300 homers in his career, and the second of those with 200 stolen bases as well, joining Carlos Beltrán.
Lindor’s homer was the second of back-to-back jacks hit by the Mets in the second inning after Ronny Mauricio homered in his third straight at-bat dating back to the two he hit in Saturday’s 7-1 win.

The New York Mets' season is ending on Sunday.
They have been out of the playoff picture for a long while, and so the final day of the 2026 MLB regular season is all she wrote for the Mets.
There won't be a lot they want to remember about what happened this year, but one player continued to be a leader as best he could: Francisco Lindor.
That included helping the Mets put up some runs on Sunday. If they were going to have the season end, they might as well hit the ball around the yard a bit more.
Lindor didn't just hit it around, either — he left the yard altogether, and it was a historic moment.
Francisco Lindor Makes Rare History
Lindor's home run on Sunday was a milestone for those who appreciate round numbers: He now has 300 home runs.
It makes Lindor the fourth infielder in MLB history with at least 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases.
Lindor has 219 steals to go with his now-300 homers.
He joins a list that also includes Alex Rodriguez, Jeff Bagwell and George Brett.
A-Rod has the most of both stats on this particular list — he hit 696 home runs and stolen 329 bases.
Bagwell ended his MLB career with 449 homers and 202 steals.
Brett just cleared the steals threshold, too, swiping 201 bags while blasting 317 homers.
Lindor joins two Hall of Famers, as well as one of the most talented players of all time in Rodriguez — whose absence from the Hall of Fame has nothing to do with his ability.
Francisco Lindor Future
The big question entering the offseason with Lindor is whether he'll be with the Mets for the long run.
A season ago, the Mets had a brutal collapse to miss the playoffs in the final week of the season.
This year, the Mets never were really even in the picture.
Yes, that also correlates with the signing of Juan Soto to a mega contract, but Lindor has obviously been a part of it, too.
What are the Mets supposed to do? They know that Lindor is still a special player — just as Soto is. But there also feels like there needs to be a vibes change heading into the 2027 season.
There's the added complication this offseason that there could be a lockout that delays the winter action as well as potentially the start of the 2027 season.
So there will be plenty of talking points beyond Lindor. Still, it's worth considering what his future looks like. He can still get the job done, but the Mets are going to want to be a lot better next season, however they can find a way to do that.

What became a disastrous season for the New York Mets will mercifully come to an end this coming Sunday afternoon.
While speaking with Mike Puma of the New York Post following the Mets' 3-1 loss at the Texas Rangers on Thursday, star outfielder Juan Soto pointed a finger at himself for the current state of the club.
"It’s definitely not what I imagined in my head," Soto said about the Mets' campaign, per Phillip Martinez of SNY. "There is nothing I can do other than blame myself. I have got to be better. I have got to be at the level to take us forward."
Soto and shortstop Francisco Lindor were supposed to help carry the Mets after team president of baseball operations David Stearns controversially dismantled the core of the club's roster last offseason. Instead, separate calf injuries limited Soto to just 108 games through Thursday afternoon. Over those contests, he slashed .274/.393/.522 with an OPS of .915, 27 home runs and 68 RBI.
That said, Soto is optimistic about the future of a team that features young talents such as Carson Benge, fellow outfielder A.J. Ewing, potential ace Nolan McLean, starting pitcher Christian Scott and others.
"We have a young core, and we have got to maintain that young core and encourage them to the right way, the right path for the future," Soto explained. "I think we are going in the right direction. Look at the young core and what they have been doing their first year in the big leagues. I think it’s real special. It’s always the first and second years are probably the toughest ones of your career, so what they’re doing, I think, is very special."
One can only guess what MLB will look like whenever the expected work stoppage comes to an end, and it's unclear how uncertainty related to the state of the league will impact what clubs do this coming fall. Soto made it clear that he wants Stearns and big-spending Mets owner Steve Cohen to be aggressive in an attempt to engineer a quick turnaround for the franchise.
"We should go and get as much as we can," Soto added. "We need as much help as we can get. It was a real tough year for us, so I think we have got to go out there and grab as much as we can."
The 73-86 Mets will begin a season-closing three-game series at the rival Washington Nationals (75-84) on Friday evening.

The slugger boasts formidable numbers despite playing in just 108 games (with three still left to play), but two stints on the IL due to separate calf injuries played a part in the Mets missing out on the playoffs for the second consecutive season.
Following Thursday's game, Soto is slashing .274/.393/.522 with an OPS of .915 to go along with his 27 home runs and 68 RBI.
But Soto missed a couple of weeks in April for his first calf injury, and then a month for the second in July/August. By the time he returned, the Mets sold at the trade deadline and the team was on the verge of being eliminated from playoff contention.
Despite missing the postseason, Soto told The Post he likes the direction the Mets are headed, especially with its young core of Carson Benge, Nolan McLean, A.J. Ewing and more.
"We have a young core, and we have got to maintain that young core and encourage them to the right way, the right path for the future," Soto said. "I think we are going in the right direction.

But with expectations being high in 2027, Soto hopes the organization is active this offseason to add to the core of veterans that includes him and Francisco Lindor -- and potentially Bo Bichette if he opts in -- and the aforementioned young core so that Soto sees playoff baseball for the first time as a member of the New York Mets.
When Soto was asked about Tarik Skubal, a pending free agent and a fellow Scott Boras client, as a potential addition, the perennial All-Star said he wants to see the Mets bring in anyone who can help the team.

ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Josh Jung and Corey Seager homered, Kumar Rocker pitched five solid innings and Texas closed out its home schedule with a 3-1 win over the New York Mets on Thursday that ensured that the Rangers would remain at least tied for the AL West lead heading into the regular season’s final weekend.
Texas (79-80) stopped a three-game losing streak and moved a half-game ahead of Houston, which played Thursday night at the Athletics. The Astros (78-80) hold the head-to-head tiebreaker with the Rangers.
Texas, which finishes the regular season with three games in Minnesota, went ahead to stay on Jung’s two-run homer in the first inning off rookie left-hander Zac Thornton (5-6). Seager snapped an 0-for-15 skid when he led off the sixth with his 19th homer.
Rocker (6-11) struck out four while allowing one run and three hits. Jordan Montgomery, the fourth Rangers reliever, worked a perfect ninth for his second big league save. He’s made 161 starts and 17 relief appearances over nine big league seasons.
Francisco Lindor led off the game with a double and scored on Carson Benge’s two-out single to put New York up 1-0. Benge has a Mets rookie record 160 hits.
Thornton struck out four and walked one in his five innings. He allowed four hits and the only runs he surrendered were on Jung’s 12th homer. Seager went deep off Jefry Yan, another rookie.
Jung, who finished with three hits and a walk, is hitting .341 (15 for 44) in 11 games since coming off the injured list Sept. 12. He missed 47 games because of a left calf strain.
Up next
New York (73-86) goes to Washington (75-84) to open a three-game series Friday matching the two teams at the bottom of the NL East standings.
Texas plays Friday against the Twins, who never trailed while sweeping three games in Texas in mid-June.

item.content:encoded:
Greatest is something every player who wears a New York Mets uniform strives for. Many come and go and are either forgotten about entirely or stick somewhere in the franchise’s lore for having one amazing moment. Fans know Mike Baxter for saving Johan Santana’s no-hitter. They’ll recall the name Mackey Sasser for the inability to throw the ball back to the pitcher safely. Kirk Nieuwenhuis had his random 3-home run game. Luis Castillo lives on in infamy for dropping a routine pop up at Yankee Stadium to end the night.
A mix of greatness and defeat have followed the Mets since they were officially born for the 1962 MLB season. Several Hall of Famers have come through to call the Polo Grounds, Shea Stadium, and Citi Field home. Everything from a mix of the homegrown talent of Tom Seaver to the ill-fated signing of Justin Verlander have a part in Mets history.
While some players live on forever with statues or their numbers retired, so do individual seasons. Random, expected, and in other seasons a longtime coming, these 25 individual seasons by Mets players are the greatest in the franchise’s history. You can’t think of these players without recalling how impressive of a year they had.
The 25 best seasons by Mets players in franchise history
25) Gary Carter, 1985
Gary Carter’s entrance into Mets lore began with a bang. Literally. He homered on Opening Day 1985 and would continue to pummel baseballs throughout the season for his new ball club. Carter finished with a 6.9 bWAR (what does that mean in 1985?) plus 32 home runs and 100 RBI. Exactly matching the .853 OPS he had in his final year with the Montreal Expos the year prior, it was the early telltale sign the Mets made the right decision to make him a part of their core. Partly because the Mets made the playoffs the next year, Carter was able to jump from sixth to third in the MVP vote. Despite this, his 1985 season was the better one.
24) Cleon Jones, 1969
Offense isn’t what won the Mets the 1969 World Series. The hitting was okay, but for the longest time, Cleon Jones’ .340 batting average sat well above anyone else in franchise history. Worth 7 bWAR in part because of an atypical season where he actually rated positively as a defender, Jones had an often-overlooked year where he finished 7th in the NL MVP vote. In an era when pitching dominated, Jones’ season deserves more credit. The year might not compare as well as some Mets years with 30+ home runs or 100+. However, for the timing of when it took place and the well-aged batting average, Jones deserves the accolades.
23) Jesse Orosco, 1983
Spoiler alert! There won’t be another relief pitcher on this list. They’re sometimes hard to judge because of how many fewer innings they throw. Plus, with the ever-evolving usage of arms, they don’t stack up well against each other in different eras. Nevertheless, what Jesse Orosco accomplished in 1983 was outlandish. At 13-7 all out of the bullpen, he tossed 110 innings and had a 1.47 ERA. The effort earned him third place in the NL Cy Young. It was a one-of-a-kind type of season from a Mets reliever. Somewhat unspoken, it was only his second full season as a major league pitcher and already he was at the top of his game while helping to further define the closer role.
22) Jose Reyes, 2006
Several different Jose Reyes seasons deserve to be on this list. How does one differentiate between them? He won a batting title in 2011 but lacked in other areas. In 2006, he hit .300, had a career-best 5.9 bWAR, and stole 64 bases. Most memorable was scoring 122 runs and driving in another 81. Homering 19 times helped make this maybe his most prolific offensive season for New York. The 2006 Mets are remembered for their incredible lineup. Reyes at the very top was one of the biggest factors.
21) Edgardo Alfonzo, 2000
Edgardo Alfonzo is a beloved Mets player. He crosses off a lot of the boxes fans desire. He was homegrown, versatile, and put together some really good years for winning ball clubs. In 2000, he wasn’t the main attraction and yet the season’s totals hold up nicely all of these years later. His lone All-Star season included a career-best 6.4 bWAR with 25 home runs and 94 RBI. Both of those numbers were a little short of what he did the year previous. However, his .967 OPS overpowered any of his past seasons and remains one of the best in Mets history. Alfonzo could be trusted to hit anywhere from first to fifth in the lineup if needed.
20) Lance Johnson, 1996
The 1996 Mets weren’t very good, but they did have three players who hit really well. One of the trio put together a season that landed him on the record books and doesn’t look like it’ll be surpassed. Lance Johnson’s 227 hits and 21 triples both set single-season Mets records while leading the league. In addition to the bat, he stole 50 bases and earned himself a 1.9 dWAR. If we were ranking only seasons by Mets leadoff hitters, this would be right near the top. It’s a shame this couldn’t have occurred on a better season for the team.
19) Jerry Koosman, 1968
Jerry Koosman did something amazing. By many measurements, his best year was his first. Koosman had a small sampling in the majors during the 1967 season. The following year qualified as his rookie campaign. Koosman went 19-12 with a 2.08 ERA. He’d end up 13th in the Cy Young race and the runner-up for the Rookie of the Year, just barely, when Johnny Bench beat him for the honor. A coin toss might have been the decider for some voters as both NL rookies had a case. Koosman was later the Cy Young runner-up in 1976. Compared to 1968, his freshman year was the better of the two.
18) David Cone, 1988
Who says wins don’t matter? In 1988, David Cone went a remarkable 20-3. He wasn’t vulturing wins thanks to the help of a strong offense. Cone pitched to a 2.22 ERA while finishing third in the Cy Young race and 10th in the MVP vote. A somewhat underrated pitcher whose career spanned the lighter hitting 1980s through the Steroid Era of the 1990s, this first full season in a Mets uniform was a preview of the strikeout machine he’d later become. Fanning 212, he’d later manage to lead the league in 1990 and 1991. The ERA in 1988 was about a full run better making this the more worthy campaign.
17) Pete Alonso, 2019
Pete Alonso posted some of the most unique statistics in Mets history. The power is unmatched in a single season and career. His rookie season in 2019 featuring 53 home runs and 120 RBI also included a 5.4 bWAR and a career-high .941 OPS. The record-setting debut season out of Alonso was more than enough to make a lasting impression on Mets fans who will never stop loving him. Alonso, like some others on this list, gets bonus points for doing it as a rookie. Those 53 home runs will be tough for a veteran, let alone a player with no MLB experience, to ever match. He became the Mets home run king for a reason. His power is unmatched from just the eye test.
16) Juan Soto, 2025
Statistically impressive, the only thing missing from Juan Soto’s first year with the Mets was purpose. The team collapsed late despite Soto putting together yet another one of his token MVP-caliber seasons. Along with hitting 43 home runs and posting a league-high .396 OBP, Soto stole 38 bases. His previous single-season high was 12. Truly a one-of-a-kind type of year, the only reason this isn’t higher is because the defense slowed him down. It was the type of year to build off of while making his record-setting contract worth it to Steve Cohen.
15) Francisco Lindor, 2024
Francisco Lindor’s MVP runner-up season in 2024 needs to be experienced to fully understand. He started off as poorly as the team and managed to quite literally lead the club to the NLCS. His first 30/30 season which includes his time in Cleveland was far more complicated than just looking at the .844 OPS. Lindor was a leader and with another Gold Glove-caliber season at shortstop, managed to put together a 6.8 bWAR season. Nothing about the season was statistically insane yet Lindor seemed to do a little bit of everything well.
14) Darryl Strawberry, 1987
Strangely, the best season of Darryl Strawberry’s career with the Mets took place in a non-playoff campaign. The 1987 Mets were good, but not good enough. Strawberry set new career highs with 39 home runs and 104 RBI. Slashing .284/.398/.583 with 36 stolen bases, it was maybe the most complete year Strawberry had as an offensive player. Although he’d lead the league in multiple offensive categories in 1988, many of his 1987 totals were superior. Crossing 30 home runs and 100 RBI for the first time in his career, it was a bit of a transition from Strawberry being one of the star players to be the signature member of the Mets.
13) Bernard Gilkey, 1996
Mets fans who weren’t familiar with Bernard Gilkey’s work might assume he was always one of the better middle of the order hitters. Arriving via trade with the St. Louis Cardinals prior to the 1996 season, Gilkey cranked it up to a whole new level. It feels appropriate that he’d later make a cameo in Men in Black because Gilkey’s numbers were unworldly. He slashed .317/.393/.562 with 44 doubles, 30 home runs, and 117 RBI. The doubles are still the most of any Mets player in a single-season. The 8.1 bWAR became the best in Mets history by a position player. Created by both his bat and glove, Gilkey led the league with 18 assists, 4 double plays, 309 putouts, and ranked as the best at his position in range factor.
12) Tom Seaver, 1975
You knew Tom Seaver was coming eventually. His 1975 season earned him his third and final Cy Young Award. He probably could have had more. This season was a 7.8 bWAR campaign that had him going 22-9 with a 2.38 ERA and a league-leading 243 strikeouts. Compared to most players, it’s incredible. On the list of Seaver performances, this one is easy to overlook because even one of his non-Cy Young winning years was better. Don’t worry. Tom Terrific is all over this list with several seasons that were even better.
11) Tom Seaver, 1969
When it comes to Mets greatness, Tom Seaver is the “you haven’t seen the last of me!” in franchise history. The 1969 season ended with a championship for the Mets. In the regular season, Seaver won a franchise-record 25 games while on his way to his first Cy Young and an MVP runner-up. Neither the 2.21 ERA nor 208 strikeouts would set personal bests. This might have been the most rewarding individual season of Seaver’s career yet it falls short of his best by quite a couple. At least he got winning the big one out of the way relatively early.
10) Jacob deGrom, 2019
Speaking of Cy Young Mets seasons, Jacob deGrom got his second in 2019. His 7.2 bWAR led the league as did the 255 strikeouts. By this point, greatness was something Mets fans weren’t demanding from deGrom, it was expected. A good length away from some of those other memorable Mets seasons by pitchers like Tom Seaver, his 2.43 ERA doesn’t even do him justice for how dominant he was for his second straight season as the best pitcher in the sport. Sadly, this would end up as his final full season in a Mets uniform due to a pandemic as well as injuries in 2021 and 2022.
9) Mike Piazza, 2000
Mike Piazza had big years, moments, and numbers with the Mets. Because his defense behind the plate was never good, stats like WAR don’t rank quite as high as some others. The 2000 season was big regardless as Piazza hit .324/.398/.614 with a 1.012 OPS. The OPS was the largest in any full season for a Mets player. The year included 38 home runs and 113 RBI with the real kicker being that he had only 482 at-bats. One of those more underrated qualities about his offensive abilities, he walked 58 times while only going down on strikes 69 times.
8) Howard Johnson, 1989
Howard Johnson led the league in home runs and RBI in 1991, but it was his 1989 season which deserves a spot on this list. Armed with 36 home runs and 101 RBI, Johnson’s speed went on display with 41 stolen bases. It was his second 30/30 season with the Mets. He hit .287 as well, atypical for the .251 he hit while in orange and blue. Never the biggest star on the Mets roster during his best years in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Johnson’s powerful and speedy 1989 campaign was a special one and the best representation of what he had to offer the ball club during his peak seasons.
7) John Olerud, 1998
Each of the three seasons John Olerud spent with the Mets was special in its own way. A franchise-leading .354 batting average helps break the tie. That’s what he hit in 1998, his middle season with the club. Posting a 7.6 bWAR as well, Olerud was the 12th place finisher in the MVP race during a season where you didn’t get much attention if you weren’t hitting home runs. He had 22 with 93 RBI. More like Keith Hernandez leveled up on offense, newer statistics that emphasis on base have helped this season age better. Olerud was never the best first baseman in the league. In Mets history, he’s right there as one of the stronger overall performers.
6) Carlos Beltran, 2006
Carlos Beltran overcame a rough first year with the Mets in 2005 to put together one of the all-time great ones in 2006. The 41 home runs hit by Todd Hundley in 1996 were matched by Beltran. Posting an 8.2 bWAR, he set a new single-season high in franchise history that would only get to enjoy one season at the top. Beltran slashed .275/.388/.594. He had 95 walks and only 99 strikeouts to practically cancel each other out. The only negative about his season was how it ended. The visual of striking out looking to end Game 7 of the NLCS remains one of the first fans often think about when his name or heartbreaking Mets moments are mentioned.
5) David Wright, 2007
No Mets player has ever matched the popularity of David Wright. His 2007 season, an 8.3 bWAR campaign, set a new mark of excellence. This was Captain America at his absolute best. He hit 30 home runs, stole 34 bases, and cruised past 100 runs scored and RBI. He even hit .325 with a .416 OBP. To make sure no check boxes were left unfilled, he won a Silver Slugger and Gold Glove. The team’s collapse in 2007 likely had to do a lot with why he only finished fourth in the MVP.
4) Jacob deGrom, 2018
As much as Jacob deGrom’s ridiculously good 15-start season in 2021 was historic, it wasn’t a complete year. The 2018 season, on the other hand, included 32 starts and a magnificent 1.70 ERA. This was deGrom’s true coming out party. The debate all year was whether or not a pitcher with a losing record could win the Cy Young. He finished at 10-9 to void the conversation and was one vote shy of a unanimous decision for his first time winning the award. The season included multiple highs for deGrom including 269 strikeouts. It was the ultimate one-man army type of season in Mets history where the team was, oftentimes, only worth watching every fifth day.
3) Tom Seaver, 1971
Here’s the most ridiculous detail about the 1971 season for Tom Seaver: he didn’t win the Cy Young. A league-leading 10.2 bWAR wouldn’t have been known at the time, but a 20-10 record and league-best 1.76 ERA as well as 289 strikeouts to overtake every other pitcher in the National League should have been enough. Seaver settled as the runner-up to Ferguson Jenkins who had a 2.77 ERA and a 24-13 record. The race wasn’t even all that close with Jenkins getting 17 first-place votes and Seaver receiving 6. Both the Mets and Chicago Cubs won 83 games so it’s not as if team record mattered at all. In practically any other year, Seaver would have added more hardware to his collection.
2) Tom Seaver, 1973
If you crave Tom Seaver content, you’re in the right place. His 1973 season earned him his second Cy Young. He had a career-best 10.6 bWAR featuring a league-high 2.08 ERA, 18 complete games, and 251 strikeouts. The Mets would sneak into the postseason and then overtake the Big Red Machine Cincinnati Reds on their way to the World Series. The Mets fell short, of course, but the regular season showing by Seaver was valuable at cementing his Hall of Fame legacy. We can even include the playoffs if there was any doubt. Although he was 1-2 overall, he pitched to a 1.62 ERA in the NLCS and had a 2.40 ERA in the World Series. All the Mets were missing was league-average offense to win another championship.
1) Dwight Gooden, 1985
There shouldn’t have been any question as to what the best season by a Mets player was going to be because what Dwight Gooden did in 1985 was one of the greatest in MLB history. The 12.2 bWAR ranks as the 26th best in MLB history. It’s the best after 1913. Gooden went 24-4 with a 1.53 ERA. He led the league in complete games, innings, and struck out 268 batters. Those numbers matter a lot, as does one other one. Gooden was only 20-years-old for the entire season. This is the kind of year that’ll go unmatched by a Mets player until some sort of cosmic shift in the way the game is played or with the rule book. You can safely etch this into stone as the best.
Hall of Famers, players with retired numbers, some completely random yet memorable performances, and even a few active members cracked the list of the best individual Mets player seasons. Records were broken. Memories were made. In a couple of cases, championships were won.

ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Marcus Semien hit a tiebreaking homer in the eighth inning against his former team and Brett Baty added a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth as the New York Mets beat the Texas Rangers 7-2 on Wednesday night.



























Rookie right-hander Nolan McLean (12-10) allowed two runs and three hits over seven innings for the last-place Mets (73-85), who have won both games in Texas since ex-interim manager Andy Green was given the full-time position Tuesday.









































The Rangers (78-80) have lost three consecutive games and trail first-place Houston by a half-game in the AL West, with the Astros playing later in Seattle. They own the head-to-head tiebreaker over Texas if the teams finish with the same record.



























Semien, traded by the Rangers to the Mets last November for Brandon Nimmo, launched his 15th homer this season off All-Star closer Jacob Latz (3-4) to give New York a 3-2 lead. Semien’s first homer since Aug. 7 snapped an 0-for-13 slump.



























Latz entered with two on and one out in the seventh, the first time he’s appeared before the eighth inning since April 12.












The Mets took a 2-0 lead in the third when Juan Soto followed Francisco Lindor’s two-out single with his 27th home run off starter Cody Bradford. It was Soto’s sixth homer this year against left-handed pitching.



























After that, Soto was intentionally walked three times — twice with runners on first and second and a left-hander on the mound.












Texas tied the score at 2 in the fifth after McLean retired the Rangers’ first 12 batters. Nimmo, who spent 10 seasons with the Mets, led off with a sharp single to right field. He advanced to second on Ezequiel Duran’s groundout and scored on Jake Burger’s single. Evan Carter drove in the tying run when he beat out a potential double-play grounder.



























New York left the bases loaded in the fifth and seventh after Soto was intentionally walked. He was given another free pass with first base open and two outs in the ninth, but Bo Bichette then walked against Trevor Williams to load the bases before Baty went deep.



























Rookie LHP Zac Thornton (5-5, 3.40 ERA) starts the series finale Thursday afternoon as the Mets look for a three-game sweep. Texas hadn't announced a scheduled starter.

In a change of direction, the New York Mets hired interim manager Andy Green for the full-time job on Tuesday, giving him a three-year contract.
The team made the announcement before starting its final road trip of the year with the opener of a three-game series in Texas against the Rangers.
“Over the course of the season, it became evident that the next manager of the New York Mets was already in place,” president of baseball operations David Stearns said in a statement. “Andy has demonstrated strong leadership qualities and a unique ability to forge connections with our emerging core and distinguished veterans. I look forward to continuing our great partnership as we turn toward the 2027 season.”
Green, who managed the San Diego Padres from 2016-19, had been running New York's farm system before taking over as interim manager when Carlos Mendoza was fired in late June. At the time, Green said he wasn't particularly interested in becoming a permanent skipper again, citing the desire to keep spending time with his three daughters and saying he viewed his interim role on the bench as more of a responsibility to the club than a personal opportunity.
Stearns said Green would return to a front-office role after the season, a stance the executive stuck to in the months that followed — even as the last-place Mets (71-85) improved on the field and several rookies who rose through the minors under Green such as Carson Benge and Nolan McLean flourished in the big leagues as well.
“The players in the clubhouse have rekindled the love I have for being in the dugout," Green said at a pregame news conference in Texas.
And in the end, the Mets committed to Green and chose not to conduct a full search for a new manager this offseason.
“I think Andy is the perfect person for this job,” Stearns said.
“Andy has connected with and pushed our players to perform, despite the disappointment of the season,” Mets owners Steve and Alex Cohen said in the statement. “Over the last several months he has brought discipline, accountability and positivity to the clubhouse, attributes we were seeking in our next manager. ... We are excited for his continued leadership in the dugout.”
Coming into the season, the Mets had high expectations for a franchise without a World Series title since 1986. New York opened the season with baseball’s highest payroll at $358 million and was projected to pay an additional $124 million in luxury tax.
But the Mets underperformed early and were beset by key injuries to Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor and others. They were 34-47 at the midpoint of the season when Mendoza was fired on June 26. The team is 37-38 since Green took over.
“The last three months I think there’s been progress,” Green said. “We’ve got more to do.”
The 49-year-old Green, a former major league infielder, went 274-366 as Padres manager and finished with a losing record in all four seasons. He joined the Mets in 2023 as senior vice president of baseball development and becomes the 26th manager in franchise history.
“I am excited and humbled to officially be named manager of the New York Mets,” Green said in the statement. “When I accepted the interim role, I didn’t anticipate it becoming permanent, but the more time I spent with our players and staff, the clearer it became that this is where my passion and experience could make the greatest impact. That realization led to many conversations with my family, and together we agreed this is the right opportunity at the right time.
"I want to thank Steve and Alex for the love, ambition and commitment with which they lead this organization, and David for the trust he has placed in me. I believe deeply in what we can build together, and I’m honored to continue serving our players, this organization and the amazing Mets fans.”

September 22, 2026
The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back.
But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go.
Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full.
Interim manager Don Mattingly yanked Raley as soon as he could for Chase Shugart, and he walked in another to Ronny Mauricio – a .173 hitter at the bottom of the New York order – before a warning-track flyout from Francisco Lindor mercifully ended the frame.
The Phillies set themselves up with a bases-loaded answer of their own in the top of the seventh, after Trea Turner and Alec Bohm drew walks and Luis Arráez singled around a Kyle Schwarber groundout and a Bryce Harper strikeout. But under the pressure situation, Bryson Stott hacked a roller through the grass to second and was left slamming his helmet into the dirt as the Mets jogged back to their dugout without any damage.
The night unraveled from there. The Phillies lost to the Mets, 10-3, up in Queens. Orion Kerkering got tagged for the second straight game, letting up four more runs in the eighth, then was demoted to Triple-A after in a move that essentially exiles the struggling reliever from the roster.
They came back with a 7-2 win the next day, behind a stellar outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez that salvaged a 2-2 split in a four-game series, but with the whole weekend taken into account, it wasn't any kind of silver lining.
The Phillies are supposed to be a playoff team, and still more than likely will be, but they had four games against a Mets club living in the NL East basement right there for the taking. It was the schedule's last gimme. And yet they couldn't help but throw two of those games down the gutter, for little other reason than that they couldn't get out of their own way.
The Phillies were supposed to, or at least wanted fans to think, that they turned over a new leaf at the plate, hitting through August with the kind of small ball approach that their power-heavy lineup went out of its way to avoid for way too long, but they've since reverted back to the old habits and stubborn cold streaks that have long overstayed their welcome.
And the Phillies were supposed to have, or rather praying for, a somewhat stable bullpen after the trade deadline, but now it's so fickle and with so little time left that decisions seem destined to come down to "what starter moves into the bullpen for the postseason?"
It's been this way for five years now, through many big-money contracts that feel like they're never quite living up to the price tag, through many more failed looks at bargain-bin arms, two (and what's looking on track to be three) managerial changes, a dramatic infield shuffle mid-season, and increasingly suspect prospect development that begs an increasingly scarier question of what kind of long-term future does this club really have?
The Phillies aren't a serious baseball team. Not anymore, at least.
They're still good, sure, in the sense that they can – and again, more than likely will – qualify for a spot in October.
But really, they could've locked that spot up a week ago.
Instead, they're 8-10 through September. They punted any possible shot at the NL East title out the window once they let the Braves go 4-3 against them across their final two series, and left a Diamondbacks club that has notoriously broken their hearts before with a faint (and therefore dangerous) glimmer of hope in the final NL Wild Card chase, while leaving a best-of-three road playoff series in Atlanta as the expected prize.
And oh yeah, they do still have to play two good teams that can easily exhaust and bury them before the Phils can even think about any of what might come after.
So where really is the contender in all of this?
Certainly the Phillies are going to lean on their elite starters between Sánchez, Zack Wheeler, a revitalized Aaron Nola, and Jesús Luzardo if they can get him back in time, but at the same time, that wasn't enough against the Mets in the 2024 NLDS or the Dodgers in the 2025 division series a year later. They each countered with shutdown pitching on their side, and hung in there until the Phillies inevitably had to reach into their volatile bullpen to capitalize.
And nothing about the 2026 club suggests that this time would be any different; not when Braves and Dodgers can continue to match them beat for beat talent-wise, while having already proved that they both play much smarter games – in the field, at the plate, and even more so on the base paths – and definitely not after they just showed that they're apparently not that much further above the lowly Mets.
Brandon Marsh, who had an All-Star first half, has one extra-base hit this month.
J.T. Realmuto, once labeled the best catcher in baseball, struck out six times in the Mets series and is a .213 hitter in his mid-30s.
Luis Arráez, who has batted well above .300 for years, suddenly dipped to a .285 average as a Phillie, and while Alec Bohm is impressing with a .328 average through the month, he's never going to hit with the power many hoped for out of a former first-round draft pick at a listed 6'4" and isn't going to suddenly discover it now at age 30 while heading toward free agency.
That leaves Harper and Schwarber as the star sluggers, but at this point, as bats who can be managed around or even directly challenged, while Turner seems to perpetually volley between a $300 million force one minute and a guy who looks like he forgot how to play shortstop the next.
Here's the catch, too: the above names are either in their late 20s at their youngest or pushing well into their 30s on average, after repeated years of trying and failing to out-thump the competition, and with not many more shots expected to be left, especially now that a labor strike puts a serious threat over 2027.
The Phils had a great August, but that was always with a tough September schedule looming, which was always going to tell you what kind of team they really were.
And while there are still six games left, and a probable postseason clinch, there's enough of a picture to tell you this: The Phillies aren't serious.
They haven't been, and really, unless something way more drastic happened at the deadline or Crawford or Painter instantly became the new faces of the franchise, that reality was staring everyone in the face all winter – when the only noticeable difference to the lineup was that Nick Castellanos wasn't in it anymore.
Are they still good enough for October? To get there, sure...probably...hopefully, after this week?
But any further than that? No. They haven't shown anything to say otherwise, or that they're any different from the last two Phillies clubs that hit a hard stop.

item.content:encoded:
What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season.
The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three will ensure the Phillies’ season continues beyond Sunday. But while they remain in control of their own destiny, it won’t be easy.
To close out the final week, the Phillies host the top team in the National League in the Brewers, followed by the top team in the American League in the Rays.
Here are a few takeaways heading into the last homestand of the regular season:
Multi-inning McFarlane
The circle of trust in the Phillies bullpen right now is extremely small. The relief unit has a 5.50 ERA in September, and the club took the drastic measure of optioning Orion Kerkering to triple-A Lehigh Valley on Sunday after his struggles became untenable. Unless there is an injury to another member of the staff, he is ineligible to be on the wild-card roster.
While the Phillies’ rotation and closer Jhoan Duran are among the best in the sport, it’s the bridge between them that has been the biggest issue. The Phillies continue to hope Jonathan Bowlan (groin) will be available for the postseason. The right-hander began playing catch Sunday, and reported to the field on Monday’s off day to continue his progress.
Before the injury, Bowlan had been going through a rough stretch, having allowed a run in five of his last six appearances. Even if he were a full go, it would be hard to imagine tossing him right back into an eighth-inning, high-leverage role after spending some time on the shelf.
» READ MORE: Phillies send struggling reliever Orion Kerkering to triple A
Enter Alex McFarlane.
The 25-year-old rookie came through in a big spot against the Mets on Sunday, facing two tough opponents in Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto to get out of a seventh-inning jam. By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.
“I think it is [realistic] this time of year,” Mattingly said. “I mean, I think with Jho, you also get to the point where he’s capable of two innings. You’re just trying to get the guys that we need in the game, for as much as you can.”
So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.
The club is “very optimistic” about Luzardo’s progress from the shoulder inflammation that landed him on the injured list, according to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. Like Bowlan, he has also progressed to playing catch.
Should Luzardo remain on track to return in time for the postseason, Dombrowski said the Phillies are keeping their options open with how they deploy him. It could be as a starter, which might be a risk given his last outing will have been Sept. 7. It could also be as a reliever, a role Luzardo has less experience in, but experience nonetheless. In the deciding Game 4 of the 2025 National League Division Series, he held off the Dodgers for 1⅔ innings of emergency relief in extras, pitching on short rest.
» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

item.content:encoded:
As far as Howie Rose is concerned, this isn’t goodbye. At least not yet.
The longtime radio voice of the New York Mets called his final game for the Metropolitans on Sunday — a 7-2 Phillies win — and as he called a ninth inning for the final time, the timeless sound of the Beatles echoed throughout Citi Field. Rose, a self-diagnosed Beatlemaniac who even left the booth mid-game this season to share pleasantries with Sir Paul McCartney, didn’t let the song’s title — “Hello, Goodbye” — be the last words he ushered into this new era of Mets baseball.
“It’s not goodbye as far as I’m concerned,” Rose said on air, as fans in the stadium chanted his name loud enough to hear over the broadcast. “I’ll still be here for the ceremonies, and I don’t mean the retirement ceremonies. I mean Opening Day, and when we have Mets Hall of Fame Day, or retire a number, have an Old Timers’ Day. So I’m stepping away. It’s basically a retirement.”
An emotional Howie Rose reacts to Mets fans chanting his name as he begins his final inning: pic.twitter.com/YuB9Pvmvro
— WFAN Sports Radio (@WFAN660) September 20, 2026
Rose has previously left the door open to calling an occasional game after stepping away for good, saying last month he could see himself dropping in for one or two once he’s officially retired. But Sunday still carried some sort of finality, the culmination of a farewell Rose had already begun articulating a day earlier, hedging against a forecast that threatened to wash out Sunday’s finale.
“Whether they play tomorrow or not, I just preemptively want to say how much you all mean to me,” he told listeners Saturday, calling Mets fans “kindred spirits” who could just as easily be sitting in his chair, having grown up, like him, in the upper deck of Shea Stadium.
While the Mets pushed Rose’s formal ceremony to next season, Sunday’s game went on as scheduled anyway, giving Rose his actual final broadcast.
In honor of Howie Rose calling his last game, the Mets collectively tipped their hats towards the radio booth 🥹
“Fitting tribute for a legend” – Gary Cohen pic.twitter.com/HXwscTl04e
— SNY (@SNYtv) September 20, 2026
The Mets entered 2026 with the since fired Carlos Mendoza texting Rose in spring training to promise this would finally be his year, the World Series parade that had eluded both the team and its 52-year broadcaster. Instead, the Mets spent the year settling for far less than that vision, and Rose, whose ongoing battle with bladder cancer kept him off the road this season, called every one of his final home games anyway, unwilling to miss a single one. It was a quieter final chapter than the one he authored just two years earlier, when his calls of Francisco Lindor’s and Pete Alonso’s postseason home runs during the Mets’ 2024 NLCS run became the signature calls of his career.
While Rose certainly deserved better than a rain-postponed ceremony and a season that fell short of the World Series ending he’d hoped for, he closed out Sunday’s broadcast the way he’s closed out thousands of others: thanking his broadcast partners, his producers, and the fans who’d spent decades in the car, at the beach, or hiding a radio under the covers during a late West Coast game.
@Mets Hall of Fame Radio Voice Howie Rose says his Final Goodbye! pic.twitter.com/T4ZNZCA15j
— Mets Radio 880 (@metsradio880) September 20, 2026
“So for Keith, Ed and Pat McCarthy, I’m Howie Rose,” he said. “Thanks for joining us once again.”
